insight.otherSide: If the date passes unpaid, you're left choosing between chasing family and letting it go, and both can sting.
insight.research: In a 2021 US poll, 69% had helped friends or family with money; of those, 38% lost money and 23% said it damaged the relationship.
insight.step: Next time you lend anything, name the return date at the very start.

options.label: I'd rather give a smaller amount as a gift

insight.reveal: You'd rather give a little freely than lend a lot and keep count. Somewhere along the way you learned that loans can sour love. Giving within your limits and letting it go keeps your family ties light, and you likely sleep better for it.
insight.otherSide: Giving less than was asked can disappoint a relative who needed the full amount, and they may not understand your reasons.
insight.research: People given a little money and told to spend it on someone else felt happier that evening than those told to spend it on themselves, whatever the amount.
insight.step: This week, buy a small treat for someone with no occasion and notice how it feels.

options.label: Dread, because of last time

insight.reveal: Your stomach remembers last time, even if the family has moved on. That dread is often less about this request and more about an old one nobody ever talked through. You're generous at heart, which is exactly why it stung, and why deciding your limits ahead of time can feel like such a relief.
insight.otherSide: Old dread can make you answer before you've really heard the new request, and a fair ask may get a harder no than it deserves.
insight.step: This week, decide your answer before the next request comes, so the moment itself is easier.

questions.prompt: When do you notice that you're like one of your parents?

options.label: When I use one of their phrases

insight.reveal: Their sayings come out of your mouth, and you mostly laugh. You catch yourself using one in the kitchen or at work and grin instead of cringing. That lightness lets you carry the best bits of your upbringing forward without much effort, and leave the rest.
insight.otherSide: The less welcome habits can come along with the sayings you like, slipping through unnoticed while you laugh.
insight.step: This week, when one of their phrases slips out, smile, and tell someone where it came from.

options.label: I don't think I'm like them at all

insight.reveal: You've worked hard to become your very own person. Your life may look quite different from the one you grew up in, and that took real effort. Still, a close friend could spot a family echo in your laugh or your habits that you haven't noticed yet.
insight.otherSide: Working hard not to be like them can mean pushing away their good parts too, along with the ones you chose to leave behind.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask a close friend: "In what way am I like my parents?"

options.label: When I worry the way they worried

insight.reveal: Your worry runs in the family, in more ways than one. Some of it came down to you and some was learned up close from someone you loved, and it makes you caring, always checking that the door is locked. The hopeful part: neither is fixed, so trying something new can shift the pattern.
insight.otherSide: Worry that feels like family can be hard to question, so it may keep costing you calm long after it stopped protecting anyone.
insight.research: Pooling 50 years of twin studies on over 14 million twin pairs, genes explained about half of the differences between people across traits; the rest came from life experience and chance.
insight.step: Next time a familiar worry starts, tell yourself, "That's an old habit," and take one calm action.

options.label: When I lose my temper the same way

insight.reveal: You've heard their temper come out of your own mouth. That's a hard moment, and noticing it at all puts you further along than it feels. You're likely fiercely protective of the people around you, and that's exactly the energy that can end the pattern with you.
insight.otherSide: A temper that flares fast can frighten the very people you want to protect, and that's the part a short pause can change for you.
insight.research: Across 154 studies, calming steps like slow breathing, relaxing the muscles or taking a time-out reduced anger, while revving-up ones like jogging mostly did not.
insight.step: Today, choose your plan: "When I feel my temper rise, I'll step away for two minutes."

questions.prompt: An argument starts at a family meal. What do you do?

options.label: Change the subject

insight.reveal: You steer the table away from trouble so smoothly it hardly shows. You may have picked up this job early, and you do it at work too, turning a heated meeting towards common ground before it boils over. You're allowed to sit one out and let someone else steer.
insight.otherSide: The real disagreement never gets settled when you steer away, and it waits for you at the next meal.
insight.step: Next time, let a small disagreement run for a minute before stepping in.

options.label: Join in, I have opinions

insight.reveal: A good argument over dinner feels like closeness to you. You enjoy a lively debate with friends and rarely hold a grudge once the plates are cleared. Quieter people at the table might not know that's the game, though, and some of them could be taking it harder than you are.
insight.otherSide: In the heat of a debate, a sharp line from you can land on someone you love, and it may stay with them longer than the meal.
insight.step: At the next meal, ask someone quiet what they think before you share your view.

options.label: Find a reason to leave the room

insight.reveal: Suddenly the dishes need you, and you're grateful for them. You learned that stepping away is a quick route to calm, and your timing is often spot on, clearing plates just as voices rise. The cost is that your view rarely gets said, and someone at that table might want to hear it.
insight.otherSide: Slipping out each time means you may miss the making-up as well as the row, and the family can learn to settle things without you.
insight.research: Across 154 studies, calming activities such as taking a time-out or slow breathing tended to reduce anger.
insight.step: Next time you step away, come back with one kind sentence for the person who seemed most upset.

options.label: Stay quiet, then replay it for days

insight.reveal: You stay quiet at the table, then argue it all in your head for days. You weigh every side, including the lines you never said. Replaying keeps anger warm rather than settling it, so a calm walk or something absorbing usually helps more than another rerun.
insight.otherSide: Days of replaying can take the shine off your next family meal before it has even begun.
insight.research: People who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them got angrier; simply doing nothing calmed them better than venting.
insight.step: Next time you replay an argument, write the one thing you wish you'd said, then put it away.

questions.prompt: When did you last tell a family member you love them, in words?

options.label: This week

insight.reveal: In your world, love gets said in words, and often. Whether you grew up that way or chose it later, you make it easier for others to say it back. After a good evening you send the warm message, and it means more to the person reading it than you'd guess.
insight.otherSide: When you say it easily, you can miss a relative who finds the words hard and shows their love in other ways.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message or small gift out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, tell someone you love them in a new way: a note, a voice message, or just a look.

options.label: We show it, we don't say it

insight.reveal: Your family says 'I love you' by making sure you've eaten. You show care by turning up, fixing things and making sure nobody leaves hungry, and it's every bit as real as words. Still, someone in your life, often a younger one, may need to hear the words now and then.
insight.otherSide: Care shown only through deeds can go unread by someone who's struggling, and they may doubt your love just when they need it most.
insight.step: Next time you do something kind for family, add one sentence that says why.

options.label: I honestly can't remember

insight.reveal: You figure they already know, and they probably do. Your love shows up in steadier ways: being there, and remembering what matters. Even so, warm words mean more to the person hearing them, and feel less awkward to say, than you'd expect.
insight.otherSide: Years can pass without the words while you assume they know, and one day you may wish you'd said them more often.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment underestimated how good it would make the other person feel, and overestimated how awkward the other person would find it.
insight.step: This week, pick one family member and say it, even if it feels strange at first.

options.label: I want to, but the words get stuck

insight.reveal: The words get stuck precisely because they matter so much to you. You likely say it better in writing or in what you do, and that counts. A small, fixed moment, like the end of a call, can take the pressure off, so the words don't have to arrive all on their own.
insight.otherSide: When the words stay stuck, the people you love may have to guess, and you carry the weight of what's unsaid.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Today, make one small plan: "At the end of my next call with them, I'll say it."

questions.prompt: A family member needs help. Who usually steps up?

options.label: We share it fairly

insight.reveal: Your family shares the load, and that's partly your doing. You may well have raised the awkward 'who's doing what' question early, before anyone started keeping score, a game in which your own part always looks bigger to you. You bring that same fairness to group projects and shared homes, and people relax around it.
insight.otherSide: A fair split can feel settled for good, so when someone's life changes, your old rota may run on long after it stopped being fair.
insight.research: When couples each rated their share of household jobs, the two shares usually added up to more than the whole: we notice our own effort more than other people's.
insight.step: This week, thank a relative for the part of the load they carry.

options.label: Someone else, they live closer

insight.reveal: Distance shapes how you help, but it doesn't stop you caring. You often pitch in other ways, sorting paperwork, booking things or calling to check in. There may also be a guilt you rarely put into words, and it's usually heavier than it needs to be.
insight.otherSide: From far away you may hear only the tidy version, and the relative doing the daily care can feel alone with the rest.
insight.research: Across 142 countries, 58% of people talked daily with family or friends living with or near them, but only 30% did with those far away.
insight.step: This week, offer one specific thing you can do from afar, like a regular call or a task online.

options.label: Me, almost always

insight.reveal: You were the family's helper long before anyone said so. Friends probably call you first on moving day, and at work the extra shift lands with you. That reliability is a gift, and it lasts longer when you let someone else carry a piece of it.
insight.otherSide: You can end up running on empty as the go-to, and the rest of the family may never get the chance to step up.
insight.research: People asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: This week, ask one other family member for one specific piece of help.

options.label: Me, and I quietly resent it

insight.reveal: You keep showing up, and part of you is tired of being the only one. That resentment isn't a sign you love them less. It's usually a need that hasn't been said yet, and saying it, even once, can be the first step towards sharing the load.
insight.otherSide: Help you give while resenting it can stop doing you good, and the warmth you put in may not reach them either.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to boosted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, tell one family member one thing you need, in a single calm sentence.

questions.prompt: You and a partner disagree about something. What do you do first, or what would you?

options.label: Talk it through right away

insight.reveal: An unsolved problem weighs on you more than an awkward talk. You cool down by talking, which can surprise a partner who cools down alone. At work you clear the air before a small thing grows, and that habit saves everyone a lot of trouble.
insight.otherSide: Someone who needs time can feel cornered when you push to talk straight away, and the talk may go worse for being rushed.
insight.step: Next time you disagree with someone close, ask 'Now, or in an hour?' and let them choose.

options.label: Take time to cool off first

insight.reveal: Your first words when upset are rarely your best, and you know it. So you step away and come back with something calmer and more useful. The pause works best when the other person knows when it ends, and a simple 'give me an hour' turns your silence into a promise.
insight.otherSide: A long cool-off can leave the other person stewing alone, and the problem may feel bigger by the time you come back.
insight.research: Across 154 studies, calming activities like slow breathing or taking a time-out tended to reduce anger, while revving-up ones like jogging mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time you need space, say when you'll come back to it, like "after dinner".

options.label: Make a sharp or sarcastic comment

insight.reveal: Your wit is quick, and so is your hurt. In company, that sharp tongue makes you great fun. In a fight, though, a sarcastic line can sting a partner far more than it seemed to, and a plain 'that hurt me' usually gets you further.
insight.otherSide: Sharp words can make you look fine when you're hurting, so the real hurt may never get looked after.
insight.research: In long-running studies of couples, contempt, like mockery and eye-rolling, was the single strongest warning sign that a couple would later split up.
insight.step: Next time a sharp line is ready, try saying the feeling behind it instead: "I'm hurt."

options.label: Go quiet until it passes

insight.reveal: When things heat up, you go still and wait for the storm to pass. You're steady and slow to make things worse, which is a real strength. From the other side, though, silence can look like punishment, so a few words like 'I need time, I'm not leaving' can make a real difference.
insight.otherSide: Your silence can push the other person to chase harder, and the more they push, the quieter you may get.
insight.research: Across 74 studies, couples stuck in a pattern where one pushes to talk and the other goes quiet tended to be less satisfied and feel less close, whichever partner played which role.
insight.step: Next time you go quiet, say one sentence first: "I need some time, I'm not leaving."

questions.prompt: With a partner, how do you handle money, or how would you?

options.label: Everything shared

insight.reveal: To you, a couple is one team, wallet included. Money talks tend to come easier for you because there's less to divide. That all-in spirit shows up in chores, trips and big plans too, which works beautifully as long as you both still feel free to want different things.
insight.otherSide: With one pot, small treats of your own can start to need a reason, and that can chip away at your sense of freedom.
insight.research: In a two-year experiment, newly engaged or married couples asked to merge their money into a joint account kept their relationship quality, while couples who kept money separate declined.
insight.step: Before you pool money with anyone, agree on a small sum each of you can spend with no questions asked.

options.label: Some shared, some separate

insight.reveal: You like togetherness with a little room of your own. A shared pot for the bills and your own for treats feels just right. You may split your time, your friends and even the blanket the same way: mostly together, with one corner that's just yours.
insight.otherSide: Mixed pots need checking now and then, and if one of you earns more, what feels fair to you both can drift without anyone saying so.
insight.step: Whenever money is shared, set one date a year to check that the split still feels fair to you both.

options.label: Fully separate

insight.reveal: Your money, your call, and you like it that way. You're probably careful with what you earn and hate the feeling of owing anyone. Separate finances can still work, especially when the big shared plans, like a home or the years ahead, get talked about early.
insight.otherSide: On money, a partner may come to feel more like a flatmate to you, and big joint plans can be harder to start.
insight.step: Next time a shared cost comes up with someone close, talk about the bigger plan behind it, not only the split.

options.label: Separate, and some spending stays private

insight.reveal: Some of your spending stays quiet, and it's rarely about the money. That doesn't make you reckless. More often, a private purchase grows out of not wanting to explain or be judged, and the hiding can end up weighing more than the thing you bought.
insight.otherSide: If private spending comes to light, a partner may feel the secret more than the cost, and your trust can take a knock.
insight.research: People's minds tend to drift back to the secrets they keep far more often than they must hide them, and that drifting, not the hiding, goes with lower well-being.
insight.step: This week, mention one small purchase you'd normally keep to yourself, and see how it lands.

questions.prompt: At home with a partner or housemate, who notices what needs doing?

options.label: We both notice

insight.reveal: In your home, the invisible jobs get seen by both of you. You share the remembering and the planning, not just the doing, and that likely saves you plenty of arguments. In a shared house or at work, you spot a job and pick it up without being asked.
insight.otherSide: When you both notice, you can also clash over how a job should be done, since two noticers bring two sets of standards.
insight.step: This week, thank the person you live with for one thing they always remember without being asked.

options.label: Mostly me

insight.reveal: You carry a to-do list in your head that never quite switches off. Birthdays, bills, the almost-empty milk: you remember it all. The tiring part often isn't the chores themselves, it's being the only one keeping track of them.
insight.otherSide: Carrying the whole list can leave you tired and a little resentful, and the others at home may never learn where to look.
insight.research: Interviews with 35 couples found that the mental work of running a home, like noticing what is needed and keeping track, often goes unseen and causes friction.
insight.step: Hand one whole task to someone you live with this week, including the remembering part.

options.label: Honestly, mostly them

insight.reveal: You give credit where it's due, even when it isn't to you. Noticing less doesn't mean you care less. It usually just means you haven't learned where to look yet, and a shared list or a fixed routine can make the invisible jobs easier to see.
insight.otherSide: Letting someone else do the noticing can leave them tired in ways you may not see.
insight.step: This week, take one task you never think about and own it completely.

options.label: Me, and I keep a quiet list of who did what

insight.reveal: Your secret tally is really about wanting to be seen. You carry a lot at home, and you'd like someone to notice. But a silent scoreboard has two catches: only one person knows the game is on, and your own jobs are always easier to count than a partner's. Saying what you need works better.
insight.otherSide: A tally kept in silence can turn small jobs into proof, and every unwashed cup may start to feel personal to you.
insight.research: When couples each rated their share of household jobs, the two shares usually added up to more than the whole: we tend to notice our own effort more than other people's.
insight.step: This week, instead of adding to the list, ask plainly for one specific bit of help.

questions.prompt: A partner's phone is unlocked next to you. What happens, or what would?

options.label: Nothing, I don't look

insight.reveal: Trust comes easily to you, so there's nothing to check. You give the same easy trust to friends and coworkers, which makes you relaxed company. Because you hand it out so freely, a broken trust can hit you especially hard.
insight.otherSide: Easy trust can mean you miss early signs that something is off, and you may hear about trouble late.
insight.step: This week, tell someone close one thing you trust them with completely.

options.label: I glance if a message pops up

insight.reveal: A message pops up and your eyes follow it, like they do everywhere. You might be the one reading a stranger's book cover on the bus or eyeing the plate at the next table. It's about attention, not doubt, and it makes you great at noticing small details.
insight.otherSide: Even a quick glance can feel like snooping to a partner, and one misread message may start a worry neither of you needed.
insight.step: Next time you're curious, just ask: "Who was that?" Simple questions keep things light.

options.label: Tempted, even though I trust them

insight.reveal: You trust them, and a small worried voice still wants a peek. Both can be true at once. That urge often gets louder when you're tired or stressed, so it's worth treating as a sign you need rest more than answers.
insight.otherSide: Even an urge you never act on can colour how you feel around them, and make ordinary moments a little tense.
insight.step: When the urge comes, put the phone face down and do one restful thing for ten minutes first.

options.label: I have looked before

insight.reveal: You've looked before, hoping to feel calmer, not to catch anyone. You care a lot, and looking is a very human thing to do. The relief rarely lasts, though, because the uneasy feeling started inside you rather than in the phone, and putting the worry into words usually soothes it better than checking.
insight.otherSide: Checking in secret can leave you holding something you can't mention without admitting how you found it.
insight.research: In a 2019 US survey, 34% of people with a partner said they had secretly looked through their partner's phone.
insight.step: Next time you feel the pull to check, tell the person one worry instead, in a calm sentence.

questions.prompt: After a fight with a partner, now or in the past, who says sorry first?

options.label: Whoever was more wrong

insight.reveal: Saying sorry is about fairness for you, not about losing. Because nobody's guarding their pride, your fights often end sooner. At work you probably own a mistake before anyone has to point it out.
insight.otherSide: Who was more wrong can become its own argument, and the hurt feelings may wait while you weigh it up.
insight.research: Of six parts of an apology, admitting it was your fault mattered most to people, then offering to fix it; asking for forgiveness mattered least.
insight.step: Next time, apologise for your part even if it was the smaller part.

options.label: Me, to end the tension

insight.reveal: You can't relax while things feel wrong between you. So you usually reach out first, at home and with friends. That's warm and brave, but a quick sorry can end the fight without starting the conversation you both actually needed.
insight.otherSide: Always going first can teach a partner they never need to, and your own hurt may get skipped each time.
insight.step: Next time you apologise, add one sentence about what you actually need.

options.label: Usually them

insight.reveal: Sorry is easier for you to feel than to say. You show it instead, making a cup of tea or suggesting a walk. A partner may be doing a lot of the repair work, and an occasional 'thanks for going first' would mean more than you'd guess.
insight.otherSide: Leaving the words to them can make your care hard to see, even when the tea and the walk say it for you.
insight.research: Across 175 studies of 26,006 people, forgiving was most likely when people felt empathy for the wrongdoer, felt the hurt wasn't intended and got an apology.
insight.step: This week, be the first to say sorry for one small thing.

options.label: Nobody, we just move on

insight.reveal: Turning the page beats rereading the chapter, in your book. That keeps everyday life light, and you're likely easy to live with. Fights that never get talked about can come back in odd ways, though, like a sharp joke at dinner, so a quick 'are we all right?' is worth the awkward minute.
insight.otherSide: Without the talk, each of you is left guessing what the other still feels, and you may not find out until much later.
insight.step: After the next disagreement, ask one gentle question: "Are we all right?"

questions.prompt: At a party, a partner laughs a lot with someone new. How do you feel, or how would you?

options.label: Glad they're having fun

insight.reveal: Their happiness doesn't feel like your loss, and that's a gift. You give a partner room to shine, and they likely come back closer because of it. And when plans change at the last minute, you're usually the relaxed one.
insight.otherSide: Your own wish for attention can go unsaid, even on nights you'd like a little more of them.
insight.step: Next time you're out with someone you love, tell them one thing you'd like from the evening for yourself.

options.label: Curious who that is

insight.reveal: You turn small worries into questions, not stories. You'd sooner wander over and introduce yourself than stand there wondering. That easy curiosity protects your relationships and friendships more than you might think, because you check before you assume.
insight.otherSide: Asking straight away can come across as checking up, if your voice carries more worry than you mean.
insight.step: Next time, join the conversation and ask the new person a real question.

options.label: A small knot in my stomach

insight.reveal: You feel closeness in your body, knots and all. That knot isn't a fact about a partner; it's more often an old alarm that rings early. Being this finely tuned also means you notice when a friend is having a bad night they're trying to hide.
insight.otherSide: A knot you keep to yourself can spoil a whole evening, and it often eases once you share it in a light word.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you feel the knot, breathe out slowly and look for one sign that you're still connected.

options.label: Cooler towards them later, without saying why

insight.reveal: You go a little cold and hope they'll notice and ask why. Saying 'I felt left out' can feel risky, so the hurt comes out sideways instead. A hint like that is easy to miss completely, which means one light, honest sentence could save the whole evening.
insight.otherSide: Going cool can start a small argument about something else, while your real hurt stays hidden.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do. In tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than people predicted.
insight.step: Next time, say one honest sentence: "I felt a bit left out tonight."

questions.prompt: A partner is out, and the whole evening at home is yours. How do you feel, or how would you?

options.label: Freedom, finally

insight.reveal: You can love someone and still love an evening that's all yours. A film, a long bath, that half-finished project: the evening's likely planned before the door closes. And you're often warmer and more patient when they get back.
insight.otherSide: Treasuring your time alone can make plans together feel like something to bargain for, and a partner may take that to heart.
insight.step: This month, plan one evening alone and spend it on something you truly enjoy.

options.label: I miss them quite quickly

insight.reveal: Home, for you, is a person more than a place. You probably send a message or two before the evening's out, and feel the same pull when friends move away. That warmth makes the people you love feel truly wanted, even if a quiet evening can feel long.
insight.otherSide: If time alone always feels empty, an evening can drag, and your own interests may get little room to grow.
insight.step: Next time you're alone, try one small activity you'd never do with them around.

options.label: A bit lost, unsure what to do

insight.reveal: So much of your life is shared that alone feels a bit strange. You're likely a devoted, generous partner, and that's lovely. An evening on your own is also a quiet chance to find out which hobbies, friends and tastes are just yours.
insight.otherSide: When so much is shared, your own tastes can fade into the background, and you may struggle to name what you'd choose.
insight.research: In a study of over 93,000 people aged 65 and over in 16 countries, those with a hobby tended to report more happiness and life satisfaction.
insight.step: This week, start one small thing that is just yours: a book, a walk, a recipe.

options.label: Relief, then guilt for feeling relieved

insight.reveal: Enjoying time alone doesn't mean you love them any less. You may have picked up the idea that real love means wanting someone near all the time. Needing space is often just part of a full inner life, not a sign of a weak bond, so you can let the guilt go.
insight.otherSide: The guilt can spoil the very rest you needed, so the evening leaves you less refreshed than it could.
insight.step: This week, tell someone close that you enjoy a little time alone, and ask whether they do too.

questions.prompt: When did you last thank a partner, or the last person you dated, for something ordinary?

options.label: Today

insight.reveal: You notice the small, boring work that keeps life running. A partner who feels thanked for ordinary things tends to keep doing them, so your thanks make home run better. At work, you make sure the quiet fixer gets the credit.
insight.otherSide: Thanks given every day can start to sound automatic, and your words may lose some of their warmth.
insight.step: Tomorrow, thank someone close for one thing you've never thanked them for before.

options.label: Sometime this week

insight.reveal: Thanks lives in your head more often than it leaves your mouth. The feeling's clearly there; the habit just hasn't caught up. Tying it to a moment you already have, like sitting down to eat, can turn a nice thought into something a partner actually hears.
insight.otherSide: Thanks that stays in your head can leave someone feeling their effort goes unseen, even though you noticed every bit.
insight.research: Habits tend to grow when one simple action is repeated after the same daily cue.
insight.step: Tonight, when you sit down to eat, name one thing someone close did today and say thanks.

options.label: I'm not sure

insight.reveal: Their everyday effort may have faded into the background for you. That happens when life gets busy, and it doesn't make you a bad partner. Ordinary thanks costs nothing, though, and one 'thanks for doing that' could brighten their whole week.
insight.otherSide: When ordinary effort goes unthanked, it can start to feel invisible, and the person doing it may slowly do less for you.
insight.research: People writing thank-you letters tended to underestimate how happy and surprised the receiver would be, and to overestimate how awkward it would feel.
insight.step: This week, thank someone close for one boring, regular task they do.

options.label: I'd thank them more if they thanked me

insight.reveal: You're waiting for proof that you're seen too. Couples often get stuck right here, each keeping a silent tally and waiting for the other. Your sense of fairness is real, and the surprising part is that going first, just once, can change the whole pattern.
insight.otherSide: While you wait for their thanks, the thanks you hold back can keep the coolness going on both sides.
insight.research: In a daily diary study of couples, on days people felt grateful to their partner, both partners felt more satisfied and connected, and the lift carried over to the next day.
insight.step: This week, go first once: thank them for something small, then notice if anything shifts.

questions.prompt: A big shared decision with a partner, like moving home. How do you decide, or how would you?

options.label: Long talks until we agree

insight.reveal: Big choices are a team sport for you, not a vote. Picking a home or a trip may take you a while, but you rarely regret the path you chose together. That care makes you a great teammate at work too, even when the slow pace tries a colleague's patience.
insight.otherSide: A decision that needed a deadline can stall while you talk it through, and the waiting may cost you both a good option.
insight.research: Across 72 samples and nearly 18,000 people, couples who handle stress as a team, by listening, helping and tackling problems together, tend to be clearly happier with each other.
insight.step: For your next shared choice, each write your top three wishes, then compare.

options.label: I research and lead, they approve

insight.reveal: Nothing calms you like a plan you made yourself. You're probably the one comparing options, building the spreadsheet and lining up the visits. The risk is that a partner keeps quiet wishes to themselves, simply because your plan already looks so finished.
insight.otherSide: Doing all the legwork can leave you carrying the blame as well, if the choice turns out badly.
insight.step: Before you research your next shared plan, ask the other person what they hope for.

options.label: I mostly go with what they want

insight.reveal: Peace at home matters more to you than getting your way. You're easygoing and trusting, which is lovely. Over the years, though, a life built mostly on someone else's choices can start to feel borrowed, so it's worth putting your own wishes into words.
insight.otherSide: Going along can leave a partner making every big call alone, and they may wish you'd be more of a teammate.
insight.step: This week, share one strong preference, even about something small like dinner.

options.label: I decide in my head, then persuade

insight.reveal: You've usually made up your mind before the talk even starts. You think fast and privately, and you're often right. A partner can still feel brought in late, and that feeling tends to outlast the decision itself, so sharing your half-formed thinking early pays off.
insight.otherSide: Persuading can feel like winning, and over time the other person may stop bringing you their ideas at all.
insight.step: On your next shared decision, say your first thoughts while they're still half-formed.

questions.prompt: After a terrible day, what do you most need from a partner or someone close?

options.label: An hour of space

insight.reveal: After a bad day, you need quiet before you can talk. Right after, you might seem distant, but you're really recharging. Once you've had that hour, you open up more fully, and the talk is better for the wait.
insight.otherSide: Taking space can look like shutting someone out, if they don't know your hour of quiet ends with you coming back.
insight.step: This week, tell the people close to you how much quiet you need after a hard day, so they know it isn't about them.

options.label: Just listen, no advice

insight.reveal: You sort out a bad day by talking it through. Often you already know what to do and just need room to get there. That's why advice, even good advice, can feel like a sign you weren't really heard.
insight.otherSide: Asking only for a listener can leave you without a hand when you do need one, if people learn not to offer.
insight.research: Couples who face stress as a team, by listening, helping and tackling problems together, tend to be clearly happier with each other.
insight.step: Next hard day, start with: "I just need you to listen for a bit."

options.label: Help me fix it

insight.reveal: A clear next step calms you better than sympathy ever could. You tackle problems head-on, at work and at home. A partner who only nods along may look caring from the outside, yet it can leave you feeling alone with the mess.
insight.otherSide: Your feelings can get skipped on the way to a solution, and they may catch up with you later in the week.
insight.step: After your next hard day, ask someone close: 'Can you help me think of one step?'

options.label: For them to notice without me saying

insight.reveal: You feel most loved when someone reads you without words. You probably do exactly that for others, noticing a mood before it's mentioned. Even close partners guess wrong sometimes, though, so a small hint usually works better than a silent test.
insight.otherSide: On the days nobody catches it, you can feel unloved, even when they care a great deal.
insight.research: A review of research on adults found that receiving affectionate touch, like hugs and holding hands, tends to support closeness, calmer stress responses and well-being.
insight.step: Next hard day, say one plain sentence: "Today was rough, I need a hug."

questions.prompt: You enjoyed a first date. When do you message them?

options.label: The same night

insight.reveal: Playing it cool was never really your style. You find out quickly where you stand, which can save weeks of guessing. That same directness tends to show up with friends and at work, wherever there's something you want.
insight.otherSide: A message that same night can reach them before they've decided how they feel, and your keenness may feel like a lot.
insight.step: After your next good date, send one warm message, then leave the next move to them.

options.label: The next day

insight.reveal: You like to sleep on a good feeling before you act on it. You trust your second feeling more than your first, and it usually serves you well. It might be how you handle big purchases and big promises too: slowly, and rarely with regret.
insight.otherSide: Waiting a night is wise, but a date who hears nothing from you may read the silence as doubt.
insight.step: After a date you enjoyed, send a short 'home safe, lovely evening' that night and save the real message for morning.

options.label: I wait for them to message first

insight.reveal: You'd like to be chosen before you do the choosing. You're careful with other people's feelings, and waiting feels safer. The same pattern can turn up with friends and jobs, holding back until you're sure you're wanted, while they may be waiting for you too.
insight.otherSide: Someone you liked can drift off while you wait to be chosen, believing you weren't keen.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to think the other person liked them less than they really did, a 'liking gap' that can last for months.
insight.step: Next time you like someone, send the first message within a day.

options.label: I rewrite the message many times first

insight.reveal: You care so much that the message starts to feel like a test. Your messages at work are probably beautifully thought out too. The other person will read yours in seconds and remember only the warmth, not which version of 'I had fun' you finally sent.
insight.otherSide: Polishing every line can cost you a lot of time and calm, and the easy warmth of a quick reply may get edited out.
insight.step: Next time, write the message once, wait a minute, then send it.

questions.prompt: You get to plan a first date. What do you choose?

options.label: Coffee, easy to leave

insight.reveal: A first date with an easy way out suits you just fine. A short coffee protects your time and their feelings in one go. You sound like a practical person who likes a low-stakes trial before committing to anything big, from a new gym to a new job.
insight.otherSide: A short date with an easy exit can end before either of you relaxes, so a slow-burning spark may never get its chance.
insight.research: In speed-dating studies, over 100 measures of people's traits and wish lists could not predict who would fancy whom. The spark only showed up once they met.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone new, suggest a short plan and let it grow if it's going well.

options.label: An activity, like a walk or class

insight.reveal: You talk best side by side, not face to face. Your best conversations happen on walks, in cars or while cooking, not across a table. You likely make friends easily through shared hobbies, too, because doing something together takes the pressure off.
insight.otherSide: An activity can fill the gaps so well that your real getting-to-know-you talk never quite happens.
insight.step: On your next activity date, keep ten minutes afterwards for a drink and a proper face-to-face chat.

options.label: A proper dinner

insight.reveal: Dating, to you, is worth dressing up for. You're the type to book ahead and pick the place with care. A long meal shows you a lot, too: how they treat the staff, and how they handle a quiet moment at the table.
insight.otherSide: A long dinner can be a lot to sit through if there's no spark, and all that effort may raise the stakes for you both.
insight.step: Before your next dinner date, choose a place where leaving after one course wouldn't feel rude, just in case.

options.label: Whatever they suggest

insight.reveal: Their comfort matters more to you than your own preferences. That makes you easy, generous company. It can also leave a date knowing less about you than they'd like, so sharing even one thing you love helps them see who they're actually with.
insight.otherSide: You can end up sitting through dates you'd never have chosen, and they never learn what you'd enjoy.
insight.research: Strangers who spent 45 minutes taking turns answering slowly deeper personal questions felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: Next time someone asks what you'd like, name one real preference.

questions.prompt: Do you ever look at an ex's social media?

options.label: Never

insight.reveal: Once something ends, you close the door and keep walking. You move on fast and keep your eyes on what's ahead. Every so often, though, an old feeling may catch up with you all at once, set off by a song or a place you didn't see coming.
insight.otherSide: Closing the door fast can leave lessons unlearned, so the same pattern may turn up again for you with someone new.
insight.step: Tonight, write down one thing a past relationship taught you, and keep it somewhere you'll see it.

options.label: Now and then, out of curiosity

insight.reveal: Exes are like old chapters you reread once in a while. For you it's usually about seeing how far you've come, not wishing you could go back. That same reflective streak may have you scrolling old photos and messages now and then, too.
insight.otherSide: Even a casual look can stir up old feelings on a day you weren't expecting them.
insight.step: Before your next look, ask yourself what you're hoping to find, and if there's no answer, close the app.

options.label: Mostly after a bad day

insight.reveal: On your hard days, the past can feel like a warm blanket. You're a sentimental, loyal person, and the ex is rarely the real point. The tough day is, which is why a call to a friend tends to comfort you more than the scroll ever does.
insight.otherSide: Turning to an old flame on hard days can keep the door half-open just when you need a fresh start.
insight.step: Next bad day, message a friend before you open any profile.

options.label: More often than I'd admit

insight.reveal: That story may have ended before you were ready to let it go. You attach deeply and loyally, and checking keeps the door open a crack. That's very human, and closing it a little at a time, rather than all at once, is usually how the pull finally fades.
insight.otherSide: Each look can reopen the ache a little, and it may keep your hurt fresher for longer than you'd want.
insight.research: In a month-long diary study after breakups, love and sadness faded over time, but faded more slowly for people who stayed in contact with their ex.
insight.step: This week, mute one account for seven days, just as a trial, and see how it feels.

questions.prompt: Early on, what makes you lose interest the fastest?

options.label: They're rude to a waiter

insight.reveal: How someone treats the person serving them tells you a lot. Decency beats charm for you every time. At work, too, you're likely to watch how a new manager speaks to the cleaner before deciding what you think of them.
insight.otherSide: One bad moment can tell you less than it seems, and someone having a rough day may get no second chance from you.
insight.step: This week, notice someone who is kind to strangers and tell them you noticed.

options.label: They stay on their phone

insight.reveal: Full attention is the clearest sign of interest you know. You give it too, phone face down when you're with someone. And you can tell fast, at work and with friends, when that attention isn't coming back.
insight.otherSide: A glance at a phone can mean nerves as easily as boredom, so a shy date may lose out with you too quickly.
insight.research: Couples were observed in everyday time together. When one partner tended to ignore the other's small bids for attention, their arguments more often turned into attack and defend.
insight.step: If a date checks their phone, ask once, lightly, 'Everything all right?' before you decide what it means.

options.label: They seem too keen, too soon

insight.reveal: Slow and steady is how you like closeness to grow. Relationships built your way often rest on solid ground. The catch is that strong early interest can feel like pressure to you, even when it's really just warmth.
insight.otherSide: Backing away from early warmth can screen out the kind, open people you'd most want to keep.
insight.step: Next time someone is very warm early, give it one more date before deciding.

options.label: They like me more than I like myself

insight.reveal: Easy affection feels odd when your inner voice is harsher. You probably hold yourself to high standards at work and everywhere else. When someone likes you more than you like yourself, the gap usually says more about how hard you are on yourself than about their taste.
insight.otherSide: Doubt about their liking can lead you to end things before they've had the chance to show they mean it.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them, a gap that lasted for months between new roommates.
insight.step: Tonight, write down one thing a friend or past partner loved about you, and read it twice.

questions.prompt: Think of your past crushes. Do they have something in common?

options.label: Not really

insight.reveal: Your heart follows the person, not a pattern. You may have been surprised by who you fell for, and enjoyed it. That same open mind shows in your friends, the food you'll try and the places you want to see.
insight.otherSide: With no clear type, you may not spot the patterns you do repeat, like the same kind of ending.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask a close friend if they see a pattern you don't. Friends often notice more.

options.label: A similar look

insight.reveal: You know exactly what catches your eye first. You may have just as clear a sense of your own taste in clothes and design. The more telling part, though, is what kept you interested, which often has little to do with looks at all.
insight.otherSide: A strong first-glance type can mean you pass over people who'd have grown on you with time.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone outside your usual type, say yes to one more conversation before deciding.

options.label: They were a little out of reach

insight.reveal: The chase makes you feel alive. You're probably ambitious and driven in other parts of life too. Calm, available people can seem a little dull at first, yet they sometimes turn out to be the deepest connections you'll ever have.
insight.otherSide: Liking the chase can draw you to people who keep you guessing, and that uncertainty can wear on you.
insight.research: In one small study, women who were unsure whether a man liked them thought about him more and felt more attracted than women told he liked them a lot.
insight.step: Next time someone kind and available shows interest, give it a second chance.

options.label: They remind me of someone in my family

insight.reveal: You're drawn to what feels like home, whatever home was like. Spotting that takes real self-awareness, and it changes things. Once you can see the pull, you get to choose which parts of home you want more of, and which you'd rather leave behind.
insight.otherSide: A familiar pull can bring back old hurts as well as old comforts, sometimes before you've noticed the pattern.
insight.step: This week, name one family trait you'd love in a partner, and one you'd rather not repeat.

questions.prompt: Someone you like is replying more slowly than usual. What do you do?

options.label: Assume they're busy

insight.reveal: You don't build stories out of small silences. That makes you easy company, since you don't need constant reassurance. You likely bring the same calm to a late email from your boss or a friend who cancels plans.
insight.otherSide: Assuming they're busy can mean missing a real cooling-off, and you may keep investing after they've already stepped back.
insight.step: If slow replies carry on for a week, ask once, kindly, whether they're still keen to meet.

options.label: Check when they were last online

insight.reveal: You can turn a tiny clue into a very big meaning. You're quick to spot patterns, which is useful in lots of places. Here, though, checking usually hands you a fresh question instead of calming the first one.
insight.otherSide: Checking can take over your evening, and the worry may show in your next message before you meant it to.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you want to check, set your phone face down for twenty minutes first.

options.label: Slow my replies to match

insight.reveal: Keeping things even is how you keep yourself safe. Fairness and self-respect matter to you, and that's healthy. Matching silence with silence, though, can turn two interested people into two careful strangers before either one says what they want.
insight.otherSide: Slow replies can hide how much you like them, so they may never learn you were interested.
insight.step: Next time, reply at your natural pace and see what happens.

options.label: Quietly start losing interest

insight.reveal: You switch off early, before anything has a chance to hurt. You're good at protecting your energy, and that has its uses. It can also end something that only needed one honest question, like a simple 'is everything all right?'
insight.otherSide: Switching off early protects you from hurt, but it can also keep you from finding out what was really going on.
insight.step: Next time you feel interest fading, ask once: "Still keen to meet?"

questions.prompt: Someone great wants to make it official. What do you feel first?

options.label: Happy, let's do it

insight.reveal: Commitment feels like a door opening for you, not closing. You likely bring the same easy yes to new jobs, new cities and new friends. Your enthusiasm makes people feel chosen and safe with you, which is a lovely thing to give someone.
insight.otherSide: Saying yes quickly can skip the talk about what each of you wants, and that talk is easier for you both early than late.
insight.research: Across 43 studies of over 11,000 couples, feeling that a partner was committed was among the strongest predictors of happiness together, far more than either partner's personality.
insight.step: Before you say yes, ask what 'official' means to them, and share what it means to you.

options.label: Nervous, in a good way

insight.reveal: Big moments give you butterflies, and that's a good sign. You may feel the same flutter before a new job or a long trip. Those nerves usually mean something matters to you, not that something's wrong.
insight.otherSide: Calling every flutter excitement can make it easy for you to brush past a real doubt that deserves a look.
insight.step: When the butterflies come, write down what excites you and anything that worries you, side by side.

options.label: A little trapped

insight.reveal: Your freedom matters to you, maybe more than you say. You do best in a relationship where you keep your own friends, plans and space. That trapped feeling is often less about this person and more about the fear of losing yourself.
insight.otherSide: Feeling trapped can make you pull away from someone good, and they may take it as rejection rather than fear.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, name one thing you'd keep for yourself in any relationship, and plan to say it early.

options.label: Doubt they really mean it

insight.reveal: Even good news makes you wait for the catch. Once you commit, you're probably loyal and careful. That doubt usually comes from older stories, not from anything this person has done, and it can soften one kept promise at a time.
insight.otherSide: Waiting for the catch can make it hard to enjoy the good part while it's here, and the other person may feel on trial with you.
insight.step: Next time someone says something kind, try answering with just "thank you" and let it land.

questions.prompt: The bill arrives on a first date. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to split

insight.reveal: To you, fair is fair, even on a first date. Owing or being owed sits badly with you, in love and in friendship. After a group dinner you're happy to work out who paid what, and people trust you with it.
insight.otherSide: Splitting every bill can feel a little businesslike to a date who wanted to treat you, and they may feel turned down.
insight.step: This week, when someone owes you something small, let it go on purpose and see how it feels.

options.label: Pay, I invited them

insight.reveal: Generosity is one of the ways you show you care. You pick up the coffees or cover a friend's ticket without making a fuss. Giving lifts your own mood too, which may be part of why it feels so natural to you.
insight.otherSide: Always paying can leave a date feeling they owe you, and the evening can feel less equal than you meant.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Next time a date offers to pay, let them, and say a simple thank you.

options.label: Let them pay if they offer

insight.reveal: You're good at receiving, and that's harder than it sounds. You accept compliments and kind gestures without much awkwardness. Letting someone be generous is a kindness too, because it gives them a way to show they care.
insight.otherSide: Letting them pay every time can start to feel one-sided to a date, even if neither of you says so.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing acts of kindness gave the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being.
insight.step: On your next date, offer to cover the coffee or the next round, so the giving goes both ways.

options.label: Freeze and wait to see what they do

insight.reveal: You're so careful about the rules that the bill can feel like a test. That care makes you tactful and considerate almost everywhere else. And here's a secret: the person across the table is very likely feeling the same small panic.
insight.otherSide: The pause can feel awkward for you both, and a date may read it as reluctance rather than good manners.
insight.research: In a survey of over 17,000 single adults, most said men still pay more, yet 64% of men felt women should chip in, and 76% of men felt guilty accepting a woman's money.
insight.step: Before your next shared meal, decide what you'll offer, so the moment is easy.

questions.prompt: On early dates, how much of the real you shows up?

options.label: All of it, take it or leave it

insight.reveal: You'd rather be turned down as you than liked as someone else. You might get fewer matches that way, but better ones. The same frankness shows up in job interviews and new friendships, and the people who stay really know you.
insight.otherSide: Showing everything at once can be a lot for someone new, and a match who'd have warmed to you slowly may step away.
insight.step: On your next first date, ask two questions for every story you tell, so they get room to show up too.

options.label: A polished version

insight.reveal: You treat a first date a bit like a job interview. You read what a moment calls for and rise to it, which is a real social skill. Still, the unpolished you, odd habits and all, is probably more interesting than you give yourself credit for.
insight.otherSide: Keeping up the polish takes energy, and a date may fall for a version of you that you can't keep being.
insight.step: On your next new meeting, share one small odd thing you love.

options.label: It comes out over weeks

insight.reveal: You open slowly, but when you open, you open all the way. New coworkers and dates may underestimate you at first. Then, a few weeks in, they're surprised by how funny and deep you were all along.
insight.otherSide: Opening slowly means a date may decide before meeting the real you, and a good match can slip away early.
insight.research: Strangers who took turns answering slowly deeper personal questions for 45 minutes felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: This week, tell someone new one personal story a little earlier than you normally would.

options.label: There's one part I hide until I'm sure

insight.reveal: There's one part of you that you're scared might be too much. You're careful about who you trust, and that's wise. That hidden part, though, is usually far less strange to other people than it feels from the inside.
insight.otherSide: Keeping a part hidden can make closeness feel conditional, and you may wonder if you're loved for the whole of you.
insight.research: People asked to share something hard and honest with someone close found it more pleasant and connecting than they expected, and listeners reacted better than feared.
insight.step: This week, share a small piece of that hidden part with a friend you trust.

questions.prompt: After a few dates, you're not feeling it. How do you end it?

options.label: A short, clear message

insight.reveal: Being clear is how you're kind. You don't hide behind vague words, at work or in love, so people tend to trust you even when the news isn't what they hoped. A short, honest no is a gift, even when it doesn't feel like one at the time.
insight.otherSide: A short message can feel abrupt to someone who hoped for more, and your brevity may sting even when it's kind.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do. In tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than people predicted.
insight.step: Next time you end things, add one sentence about something you genuinely enjoyed, before the clear no.

options.label: Tell them face to face

insight.reveal: You think people deserve to hear bad news from your own mouth. That takes courage, and it's often remembered with respect long after the sting fades. You'd probably be the kind of manager who delivers hard news in person, too.
insight.otherSide: Meeting just to end it can be harder on the other person, who has to hold their face together in public while you talk.
insight.step: Next time you must give hard news, think of one kind true sentence to start with.

options.label: Reply less and less until it fades

insight.reveal: Drifting away feels kinder to you than saying something that hurts. You're gentle and you hate conflict, which is understandable. The fade, though, often leaves the other person guessing far longer than one short, kind message from you would.
insight.otherSide: A small guilt can follow you each time their name pops up, long after it's over.
insight.step: Next time, send one short honest line: "I enjoyed meeting you, but I don't feel a match."

options.label: Keep going a bit longer so they're not hurt

insight.reveal: You carry other people's feelings like they're your own. That kindness is real. The same habit can keep you in jobs, plans and friendships long after you already know they're over, and staying out of guilt isn't really a gift to anyone.
insight.otherSide: Staying on to spare their feelings can lead them to hope for more, so your eventual goodbye may hurt them harder.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to boosted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, notice one thing you're doing only to avoid disappointing someone, and plan a kind way out.

questions.prompt: A stranger on the street looks lost. What do you do?

options.label: Walk over and ask if they need help

insight.reveal: You act first and wonder later. You speak up when a meeting stalls, or ask the driver which stop it is instead of squinting at the signs. Now and then you rescue someone who was only checking their map, and you both end up laughing about it.
insight.otherSide: Acting first means you sometimes sign up for a long detour before you've checked whether you have the time.
insight.step: When you next spot someone looking lost, give it two seconds first, then ask, 'Finding your way all right?'

options.label: Help if they ask me

insight.reveal: You'd hate to barge into a stranger's day uninvited. Once someone asks, though, you go all in and might walk them the whole way there. Most lost people feel relief, not intrusion, when a kind face offers first, so your politeness can afford a step forward.
insight.otherSide: Waiting to be asked can mean someone too shy to ask walks on, still lost, a few steps away from you.
insight.step: Next time you see someone confused, make eye contact and smile. That alone invites them to ask.

options.label: Assume someone else will help

insight.reveal: You admitted something that usually stays unspoken. In a crowd, it's easy to assume someone else will step in. In real life, though, someone usually does step in, and noticing your own pause is how you become the person who goes first.
insight.otherSide: Waiting for someone else can leave you replaying the moment later, wishing you'd crossed the street yourself.
insight.research: In 219 real street conflicts caught on camera in three countries, someone stepped in to help in 9 out of 10, and more bystanders meant help was more likely, not less.
insight.step: Next time you think "someone else will", be that someone, once.

options.label: I want to help but feel too shy

insight.reveal: Your heart is already halfway across the street. You spot someone's trouble from a distance, then the words get stuck, and later you replay it and wish you'd said something. One ready line, like 'Are you looking for somewhere?', can carry you the rest of the way.
insight.otherSide: Shyness can let a kind moment pass so fast that the person never knows you cared.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, make a when-then plan: "When I see someone looking lost, I'll ask: can I help you find something?"

questions.prompt: A neighbour you barely know asks you to water their plants for a week.

options.label: Say yes, happily

insight.reveal: To you, a spare key is the start of a friendship. You take in deliveries, feed the cat next door and somehow get invited whenever there's food. Your key ring may well hold more keys than you have doors.
insight.otherSide: Saying yes so readily can mean other people's keys, pets and plants start to fill weeks you'd hoped to keep free.
insight.research: On days when people had more chats with casual acquaintances, not just close friends, they tended to feel happier and a stronger sense of belonging.
insight.step: This week, introduce yourself to someone who lives near you but whose name you don't know yet.

options.label: Say yes, then worry I'll forget

insight.reveal: You say yes, then set three reminders for one watering can. A promise sits heavy with you, even a small one, and the plants will probably do better with you than with their owner. The only cost is your own calm, which deserves the same care you give those plants.
insight.otherSide: The worry can make you slow to say yes to the next small favour, even one you'd enjoy doing.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ('When X happens, I will do Y') had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you say yes to something small, tie it to a daily moment: 'When I put the kettle on, I'll water the plants.'

options.label: Find an excuse

insight.reveal: Your home is your quiet place, and you guard the door. You know the people next door by face more than by name, which suits you fine. The catch is that small swaps of help are how strangers turn into people you can call when your own pipe bursts.
insight.otherSide: Each excuse can leave a small knot of guilt in you, and it may make the next hello a little stiffer.
insight.step: This week, do one tiny good turn for someone nearby that fits your own schedule.

options.label: Say yes, then wish I'd said no

insight.reveal: Your yes often comes out before you've checked how you feel. A week of someone else's chores seems easier than five awkward seconds of no, so your calendar fills with other people's plans. The kindness is real. It just deserves a quick pause first.
insight.otherSide: Help given with a heavy heart can sit between you and the neighbour, even if they never knew you minded.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Next request you get, say "Let me check and get back to you" before answering.

questions.prompt: Some unexpected extra money arrives. What would you enjoy most?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: You'd rather have breathing room than a new thing. You can happily wait for the things you want, and that patience adds up over the years. The tricky part for you is the spending: even a treat you've fully earned can feel like it needs a good excuse.
insight.otherSide: Saving it all can mean good luck never quite gets felt, and your chance to share it with someone may pass.
insight.step: Next time extra money turns up, spend a tiny part on something purely fun and notice how it feels.

options.label: A treat for myself

insight.reveal: You celebrate good luck while it's still warm. You're fun to be around when things go right, and you don't wait for a perfect moment to enjoy life. One small twist: looking back, a good evening out will probably make you happier than a new thing.
insight.otherSide: Spending while the luck is still warm can mean it's gone before you've decided what would truly please you.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money brings more joy when spent on experiences, on others, on many small treats rather than one big one, and on things to look forward to.
insight.step: Next treat, choose an experience instead of an object and compare how long the happy feeling lasts.

options.label: A day out or trip

insight.reveal: You'd trade a new gadget for a good story any day. What you keep from a year is moments: a walk, a meal, a trip with someone you like. Ask you about your best day this year, and you'll describe a place, never a purchase.
insight.otherSide: Money spent on a day out is gone by evening, so a leaner month later can feel a little tighter for you.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, plan one small outing with someone you like: a new walk, or a meal somewhere you've never tried.

options.label: Quietly spending it on someone else

insight.reveal: Your best gifts are the ones nobody knows came from you. You remember the thing a friend mentioned wanting months ago, then turn up with it on an ordinary day. A quiet gift lifts you more than anything you'd buy yourself, which is a lovely kind of selfish.
insight.otherSide: Giving it away can leave your own needs at the back of the queue, and they matter too.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, buy a small surprise for someone and don't tell anyone else.

questions.prompt: Where are you with volunteering?

options.label: I do it regularly

insight.reveal: Giving is part of your week, not a mood that comes and goes. Through it you've likely made friends of every age, people you'd never have met otherwise. On a slow, rainy weekend, you have somewhere to be and someone who's glad you came.
insight.otherSide: A regular commitment can turn into one more duty on a tired week, and it may be hard for you to step back without guilt.
insight.step: Next time you volunteer, bring one friend along.

options.label: Now and then, when someone asks

insight.reveal: A friend's ask moves you more than any poster ever could. You help through people rather than causes, so your help tends to land exactly where it's needed. When someone's plans fall apart, they know they can call you.
insight.otherSide: Waiting to be asked leaves your help in other people's hands, and a cause you'd love may never come your way.
insight.step: This week, ask one friend if there's anything they could use a hand with.

options.label: I keep meaning to start

insight.reveal: Your care is real, but 'someday' keeps winning. Full weeks push good plans to the back, and there may be a website or two you saved and never opened again. Picking an actual day, place and time is usually what turns 'soon' into a first visit.
insight.otherSide: Meaning to for a long time can turn a good wish into a small guilt, and guilt rarely gets you through the door.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, try a when-then plan: "When I finish breakfast on my day off, I'll look up one place nearby that needs help."

options.label: I help in private, informal ways instead

insight.reveal: Your kindness rarely comes with a name tag. You drive people places, drop off meals and fix things without fuss, and nobody keeps a list. That everyday kind of help is far more common than signing up to volunteer, and those close to you may only notice how much you carry once you're away for a week.
insight.otherSide: Because nobody keeps a list, you may give more than you can spare, and no one around you will think to say stop.
insight.research: In 2023, 28% of Americans volunteered through an organisation, but 54% informally helped neighbours, like running errands or lending tools.
insight.step: This week, when someone thanks you for a lift or a meal, accept it with a simple 'You're welcome' instead of waving it away.

questions.prompt: You helped someone a lot and nobody noticed. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, that wasn't the point

insight.reveal: You'd help the same way with the lights off. Whether or not anyone's watching, you act the same, and people sense it. At work you get trusted with the sensitive stuff, and friends bring you the secrets they'd tell nobody else.
insight.otherSide: Wanting nothing back can make it hard for you to accept thanks, or help, when it finally comes your way.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, do one small helpful thing that nobody will ever trace back to you.

options.label: I find a way to mention it

insight.reveal: Wanting your effort to be seen is completely fair. You're good at making invisible work visible, the kind that otherwise vanishes into 'it just got done'. A hint can get missed, though, while a plain 'I worked hard on that' usually lands and feels better too.
insight.otherSide: If mentioning it becomes a habit, people may start to hear the reminder more than they see your help.
insight.step: Next time you feel unseen, say simply: "I worked hard on that, I'd love a thank-you."

options.label: A little hurt, honestly

insight.reveal: That little sting shows how much care you put in. You put more thought into helping than ever shows: the timing, the details, the extra step nobody asked for. Hoping to be noticed doesn't make it less generous, and it shows you how much a simple thank-you can mean.
insight.otherSide: That sting can linger longer than the help took, and it may make you hold back a little next time.
insight.research: People writing thank-you letters underestimated how happy and surprised the receivers would be, and expected them to feel far more awkward than they really did.
insight.step: This week, thank someone for an effort nobody else mentioned, and notice how it feels.

options.label: I remember it for a long time

insight.reveal: You keep a quiet record of the help nobody thanked. You notice what's unfair straight away, and you'd never short-change anyone yourself. Over the years, though, that record can grow heavier than the help ever was, and you're allowed to set some of it down.
insight.otherSide: Remembering every unthanked favour can slowly cool how you feel about people you were once glad to help.
insight.step: This week, pick one old unthanked effort and let it go with one sentence: "I did that because I wanted to."

questions.prompt: You're struggling with something. How easily do you ask for help?

options.label: Easily

insight.reveal: Asking for help feels as normal to you as offering it. That makes others feel trusted and useful, so they tend to show up fast. You sort out problems sooner because you don't struggle alone, and you rarely carry something heavy longer than you have to.
insight.otherSide: Asking easily can sometimes land on someone who finds no hard to say, so their yes may cost more than you see.
insight.research: In studies with over 14,000 strangers, people asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: Whenever you ask a favour this week, add 'and it's fine to say no', and mean it.

options.label: Only for practical things

insight.reveal: You'll ask for help carrying boxes, but rarely for comfort. Help with jobs feels fair and easy to repay; help with feelings feels like owing too much. Yet the person who turns up to carry boxes would often happily sit and listen too.
insight.otherSide: Carrying the heavy feelings on your own can make a hard month feel longer, even with plenty of help on the practical side.
insight.step: This week, tell one person how you're really feeling, not just what you need done.

options.label: Only when it's almost too late

insight.reveal: You hate the idea of your problems landing on anyone else. So you handle a surprising amount alone, and you're quick to help when someone else is struggling. Meanwhile your own pile keeps growing out of sight, and things are much easier to ask about while they're still small.
insight.otherSide: Leaving it late can make asking feel like an emergency, when an early word would have felt easy for you both.
insight.step: This week, ask for help with one thing while it's still small.

options.label: I'd rather help someone else

insight.reveal: Giving care feels safer to you than needing it. In a crisis you're likely the steady one people call, knowing what to bring and what to say. Being on the receiving end can feel exposed, but the people who love you would welcome a turn at looking after you.
insight.otherSide: Always being the helper can leave you running on empty, with no one quite sure how to look after you in return.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person being helped.
insight.step: This week, let someone do one small thing for you, and simply say thank you.

questions.prompt: A coworker or classmate is clearly overwhelmed. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to take something off their plate

insight.reveal: For you, help means rolling up your sleeves. Your team leans on you more than they ever say. When a project gets rescued at the last minute, your name tends to come up, even if you'd rather it didn't.
insight.otherSide: Taking on their tasks can overload your own plate, and you may become the person everyone hands things to.
insight.step: Next time you offer help, name one specific task instead of saying "let me know".

options.label: Bring them a coffee or snack

insight.reveal: A well-timed snack is your way of saying 'I see you'. You remember how each colleague takes their coffee, and who skips lunch when things get busy. Big rescues get the praise, but your small comforts often get someone through a long afternoon, and giving them probably lifts your mood too.
insight.otherSide: A snack is lovely, but it can stand in for the harder question of whether they need real help from you.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: With the next coffee you bring someone, add one question: 'Is there anything I can take off your plate?'

options.label: Wait until they ask

insight.reveal: You trust people to know what they need. You'd make the kind of manager who never hovers, and you give others the space you'd want yourself. Overwhelmed people rarely ask, though, which is partly how they got swamped, so one gentle question can open the door.
insight.otherSide: Respecting their space can look like not noticing, and they may feel more alone than you'd ever intend.
